analysis.title: US Midterm Elections: what to expect and what the market impact could be
key_insights: CACIB puts the odds at 65% for a Democratic sweep, 25% for a Democratic House with a Republican Senate, and 10% for a Republican sweep. A Republican House with a Democratic Senate is called highly unlikely.
Trump's overall approval is below 40%, more than 20ppt underwater. He is -32.4ppt on the economy, -43.8ppt on inflation and -10.6ppt on immigration.

Democrats lead the generic congressional ballot by more than 8ppt, against a 2.6ppt Republican win in the 2024 House vote. That is a swing of about 11ppt. CACIB puts the odds of a Democratic House at around 90%.

Republicans hold the House 220-215 (vacancies assigned to the prior party), so Democrats need a net gain of at least three seats. Redistricting limits the competitive seats to the 20s, which makes a 40+ seat wave unlikely.
Republicans hold the Senate 53-47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats, since Vice President Vance breaks a 50-50 tie. CACIB puts Democratic Senate odds at around 65%.
Legislative gridlock is expected if Democrats win the House, whatever happens in the Senate, because of the filibuster and the presidential veto. A veto override needs two-thirds of both chambers.

The main effect of a Democratic Senate would be the power to block judicial and other appointments. It would also add oversight and investigations. CACIB sees a good chance of another impeachment but treats it as noise, since removal needs two-thirds of the Senate.

A government shutdown is a risk either way, and CACIB sees a decent chance of another one next year. Tariff policy and foreign policy are not expected to change much, because Trump relies on previously delegated authority.

Rates: divided government would reduce the odds of major spending programmes and tax cuts. That would ease term premium pressure and favour lower long-end yields and a flatter curve. Front-end yields stay high because energy prices are elevated and the Fed is expected to hike further.

The FY2026 federal deficit was USD1.99trn (about 6% of GDP), on USD7.4trn of spending (+6%) and USD5.4trn of revenue (+3%). The prior deficits were USD1.775trn (FY2025) and USD1.817trn (FY2024). CBO projects debt-to-GDP rising from 100% to 120% within a decade.

CACIB's regression of the 5-10Y curve on the 2Y yield gives a constant of 2.27, a 2Y coefficient of 0.55 and a coefficient of -2.32 on a third variable. R^2 is 76%. Inflation expectations and the deficit path have been the main drivers of term premium recently.

FX: since 1976, a Democratic Congress with a GOP president has coincided with USD weakness in the months after the vote. A GOP president and Senate with a Democratic House has coincided with USD rallies, most recently after the 2018 midterms.

CACIB's USD view is that gridlock and fading fiscal support are downside risks to US growth and the dollar. The main scenario is cyclical convergence between the US and the rest of G10, with Fed cuts in H2 2027. The risk scenario is an AI boom-bust ending in a global selloff, a persistent energy shock, or a US recession or stagflation.
Emerging markets: the midterms are not seen as a game changer. The three issues are fiscal and growth effects, Iran and oil prices, and the AI trade. The direction of each is ambiguous.

EM data is resilient. Retail sales and industrial production are holding up, and EM exports are accelerating on electronics, chips and AI in Asia, commodity prices in Latin America and the Middle East, and German-linked components in Central Europe.
China GDP growth is expected at 4.6% in 2026. CACIB sees the midterms as no game changer for China because both parties favour capping its geoeconomic rise.
The EM-DM carry gap is described as decent. The EM-US 3M implied yield gap is 311bp, from 430bp EM implied yield against 120bp for US 3M SOFR.

macro_indicators.interpretation: A very large deficit for a period without recession, which keeps pressure on Treasury term premium. Divided government would limit new spending and tax cuts.

macro_indicators.reading: 100% now, rising to 120% within a decade
macro_indicators.interpretation: Debt keeps accumulating even with stronger growth. Stabilising it would take 6% real GDP growth with 5% interest rates.
Front-end yields stay high on elevated energy prices and further Fed hikes, then ease late in 2027.
Long-end yields stay above 5% through most of 2027, with a gridlock-driven easing in term premium at the margin.
Long-end yields remain elevated, with the fiscal path as the main driver.
The curve is nearly flat from 2Y to 10Y in the forecast.
Targeted stimulus and exports support growth, and the US election outcome is not expected to change it.

macro_indicators.reading: Additional rate hikes expected near term, cuts in H2 2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: Elevated energy prices keep the Fed hawkish near term. Fiscal dominance and global disinflation lead to cuts later, converging with the rest of G10.

risk_factors: A government shutdown next year, with the possibility that Trump vetoes funding legislation from a Democratic Congress.
An AI boom-bust cycle ending in a global market selloff.
A persistent negative energy shock that hurts global growth.
A US or global slowdown, possibly recession or stagflation.
Fiscal deterioration, with a deficit near 6% of GDP and rising debt, pushing up term premium.
Trump becoming more assertive on Iran, which would push oil prices up.
A cooling AI trade that caps risk appetite.
charts_described: Trump approval rating has dipped below 40%, more than 20ppt underwater against disapproval.
Generic congressional ballot: Democrats lead by more than 8ppt, against a 2.6ppt Republican win in the 2024 House vote.

Key Senate races table: North Carolina (Cooper +10.6 in the RCP average, Likely D), New Hampshire (Pappas +6.5, Lean D). Toss-ups: Alaska (Peltola +1.2), Iowa (Turek +0.6), Kansas (Marshall +0.3), Maine (Jackson +1.4), Michigan (El-Sayed +1.9), Ohio (Brown +3.3) and Texas (Talarico +1.5).
Regression table for the 5-10Y curve on the 2Y yield: coefficients 2.27, 0.55 and -2.32, R^2 76%, F statistic 811.1 and 499.0.
vol_and_positioning: Market betting odds show investors expecting a Democratic sweep of Congress.
Foreign investors have been buying US stocks but not US Treasuries.
Past government shutdowns show mixed USD performance across G10 currencies and gold in the month before and the one to two months after.
geopolitical: US midterm elections on 3 November 2026, with a Democratic House expected.
Iran: a Democratic sweep could mean less leeway for Trump to spend on Iran and less pressure on oil. Alternatively he could become more assertive to rally his base, which would push oil higher.
Foreign policy: the president has greater authority, so no major shift is expected from the election. Democratic control of the Senate could still frustrate Trump's foreign policy.
US-China: a bipartisan consensus to cap China's geoeconomic ascent means the midterms are not a game changer for China.
Middle East conflict and an energy shock are cited as risks and as features of past episodes of USD weakness.

tension_points.bull_case: Historically, a GOP president with a GOP Senate and Democratic House has coincided with USD rallies, as after the 2018 midterms, when the US economy was recovering and the Fed was hawkish.
tension_points.bear_case: A Democratic Congress with a GOP president has coincided with USD weakness after the vote (1985 Plaza Accord, early George H W Bush, George W Bush's second term). Gridlock and fading fiscal support are downside risks to US growth and the USD.

tension_points.bull_case: Divided government cuts the odds of major spending and tax cuts, easing term premium and supporting lower long-end yields and a flatter curve.
tension_points.bear_case: The deficit is about 6% of GDP and debt-to-GDP is projected to reach 120%. Front-end yields stay high because energy prices are elevated and the Fed is expected to hike further.

tension_points.bull_case: Less leeway to spend on Iran after a Democratic sweep could mean less pressure on Iran and lower oil.
tension_points.bear_case: Trump could become more assertive on Iran to galvanise his base, which would push oil prices higher.
